issues.section: 11.3 What counts as validated / Hands-on: Labs 11.1 and 11.2
issues.quote: All five agree within 0.4σ. ... The reference systematic is our assumption (1%)
issues.problem: The agreement comes from an assumed, uncorrelated 1% reference error that PDG does not quote. Stat-only pulls are −2.0, −1.0, −2.2, −1.0, −0.2 (all same sign, χ²=10.8/5, p=0.06). With the 1%, χ²=0.28/5, i.e. agreement this good happens 0.2% of the time: the error model is inflated. The 1% (mean excitation energy) is fully correlated across energies, so adding it per point independently is wrong. The hero ('dE/dx vs PDG ≤ 0.4σ at 5 energies') and README repeat the inflated headline.
issues.fix: Show stat-only pulls and χ²/ndf, fit the 1% as one correlated normalisation nuisance, report the residual −0.1% to −0.4% trend, and teach 'too-good χ²' as a validation smell. Change the hero to 'agrees within 0.4% (χ² ...)'.

issues.section: Hands-on: Labs 7.1 and 7.2 · Check the integrator before blaming the physics
issues.quote: The 1 GeV σ differs from step 3 (0.0031 against 0.0040) because the run produces different random scattering, not because of integration
issues.problem: The same page states 'about ±3% relative on σ'. A 25% change is ~8× that error, so it is not an ordinary fluctuation; np.std on 1000 events is being driven by a few scattering/δ-ray tail events. The toy uses the half-width of the central 68%; reconstruct.py uses np.std, so toy and lab quote different widths.
issues.fix: Use the central-68% half-width in reconstruct.py with a bootstrap error, then compare runs in units of that error; explain the tail.

issues.section: Hands-on: Labs 7.1 and 7.2 · Lab 7.2: same field integral, different field
issues.quote: The bias moves from −0.05% to about +0.13%, roughly 15σ at 1 GeV and 5σ at 20 GeV
issues.problem: The σ used is σ/√N of one sample. The bias is a median (error ≈1.25σ/√N) and the shift is a difference of two independent runs (×√2): ~9σ at 1 GeV. At 20 GeV the baseline bias is +0.0002 (step 3), not −0.0005, giving a shift of 0.0013 ≈ 2σ (3σ against step 4's −0.0004).
issues.fix: Quote the shift with the two-sample median error and name which baseline is used; '≈9σ and ≈2–3σ'.

issues.section: Hands-on: Lab 4 · Compare with Bethe
issues.quote: The three middle points agree with the formula to 0.5%.
issues.problem: In σ the 200 MeV point (2.065 ± 0.0019 vs 2.055) is ~5σ off. Week 1 teaches 'quote the difference in units of σ', and this page switches to percent without naming the formula's own uncertainty (no shell, Bloch, Mott corrections).
issues.fix: Give pulls and add 'the leading Bethe form is good to ~0.5–1% here, which is the systematic that makes these points agree'.

issues.section: Practice quiz · Q5

issues.problem: The course's own Geant4 table (code/week06/cut_thresholds_g4_11.4.json, used by the explainer) gives e⁻ thresholds of 14.5 keV at 10 µm, 1.74 keV at 3 µm, and the 990 eV floor only at 1 µm. The stem is false for e⁻ (true for γ below ~30 µm).

issues.section: 11.1 Debugging is a tree / Hands-on · Students: run every branch
issues.problem: 0.0050 ± 0.0050 is k = 1 of 200 with the binomial σ that Week 1 (MC0004) says fails near the boundary. Against main (0.0193 ± 0.0010) it is 2.8σ low — the page's own L0 threshold is '2–3σ'. 'Nothing broken' rests on one column (0.7σ) and ignores three columns tested at once.
issues.fix: Use a Wilson/Clopper-Pearson interval for small k, mention the look-elsewhere effect across columns, and keep the verdict but justify it.

issues.section: 3 Muons in rock
issues.quote: in standard rock the two are equal near 500 GeV
issues.problem: PDG's passage-of-particles tables give the muon critical energy for standard rock as 693 GeV; ~500 GeV is the a/b ≈ ε approximation of the cosmic-ray review. Both are PDG; say which.
issues.fix: 'near 500–700 GeV (PDG: a/b ≈ 500 GeV; Eμc = 693 GeV)'.

issues.section: 3 Muons in rock · Scattering: the second effect
issues.quote: A 3 GeV muon crossing 1 m of standard rock is deflected by about 0.9°
issues.problem: 0.89° is Highland θ0, the RMS of the plane-projected angle at p = 3 GeV/c; the space angle is √2 larger and tails are non-Gaussian. Engineers will read it as 'the' deflection.
issues.fix: 'an RMS of about 0.9° in each projection (≈1.3° in space) at 3 GeV/c'.

issues.section: Watch a hill filter the sky (also primer 4 Muography)
issues.quote: toy spectrum dN/dE ∝ E−2.7 above 1 GeV ... (real sea-level spectra are flatter below about 10 GeV)
issues.problem: Honest label, but it omits that the real spectrum steepens towards E^−3.7 above ~100 GeV, which is exactly the regime of >150 m of rock. The toy overstates deep transmission.
issues.fix: Add 'and steeper above ~100 GeV'.

issues.section: Background · Significance of a feature
issues.quote: the feature stands out by about ΔN/√N standard deviations
issues.problem: For muography exposures of weeks to months, the flux-model and rock-density systematics (the primer quotes 10–15% on the flux) exceed √N, and significance stops growing as √time. Juniors will over-promise to clients.
issues.fix: Write ΔN/√(N + (fN)²) and use the planner's systematic floor in a muography example.

issues.section: 5 What Geant4 does for a muography project
issues.quote: primary generator (cos²θ toy; CRY, EcoMug or a parameterisation in practice) | 1, 2, 5
issues.problem: No week teaches a realistic generator, transport through tens to hundreds of metres of layered rock, or scattering muography. The muography track (Weeks 1–8, 11, 12) never produces a flux-ratio map, the deliverable my staff need.
issues.fix: Add a muography lab (generator + layered rock + void + exposure estimate, validated against an open-sky rate) replacing Weeks 9–10 on that track.
